Please solve this issue: We're building backend for a helpdesk SaaS for businesses and their customers.
Use Rails in API-only mode; the frontend is a separate app.
Ruby, Rails, Puma, and PostgreSQL are installed. If you need anything else, install it yourself.
Use `DATABASE_URL`. Work in `/app`.

Customers should also be able to email support and reply from their mail client. Add this with
Action Mailbox. Each business receives mail at its subdomain under `HELPDESK_SUPPORT_DOMAIN`,
default `support.example.test`; Acme gets `acme@support.example.test`.

Use Action Mailbox's relay ingress at `/rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails`, authenticated
with `RAILS_INBOUND_EMAIL_PASSWORD`. In test, process incoming mail before the request completes
so a separate worker isn't needed.

Incoming mail should open a ticket with its subject and plain-text message.

Find the business from the recipients, including Cc. Ignore mail addressed to multiple businesses.
Reuse an existing customer, or create one and send a verification email so they can later use the portal.
Receiving email shouldn't verify their account.

When staff post a public reply to an email-origin ticket, email it to the requester. Give each
ticket a private reply address at the support domain, so the customer's next email returns to
the right conversation. Only the requester may reply by email. Replies reopen pending or solved
tickets; a new message to the plain support address opens a new ticket.

Deduplicate deliveries by Message-ID. Invalid deliveries must not block a later valid retry.
Ignore automated/list mail.

require_relative "helpdesk_config"

class CorsMiddleware
  DEFAULT_ALLOW_METHODS = "GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD"
  DEFAULT_ALLOW_HEADERS = %w[Authorization Content-Type X-Helpdesk-Account Accept].freeze
  MAX_AGE = "7200"

  def initialize(app)
    @app = app
  end

  def call(env)
    origin = env["HTTP_ORIGIN"]
    origin_allowed = !origin.nil? && !origin.empty? && origin == HelpdeskConfig.frontend_origin

    if env["REQUEST_METHOD"] == "OPTIONS"
      return handle_preflight(env, origin, origin_allowed)
    end

    status, headers, body = @app.call(env)
    append_vary_origin(headers)

    if origin_allowed
      headers["Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = origin
    end

    [ status, headers, body ]
  end

  private

  def handle_preflight(env, origin, origin_allowed)
    unless origin_allowed
      return [ 403, { "Vary" => "Origin" }, [] ]
    end

    requested_headers = env["HTTP_ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_HEADERS"].to_s
      .split(",")
      .map(&:strip)
      .reject(&:empty?)

    merged_headers = DEFAULT_ALLOW_HEADERS.dup
    requested_headers.each do |header|
      merged_headers << header unless merged_headers.any? { |h| h.casecmp?(header) }
    end

    headers = {
      "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" => origin,
      "Access-Control-Allow-Methods" => DEFAULT_ALLOW_METHODS,
      "Access-Control-Allow-Headers" => merged_headers.join(", "),
      "Access-Control-Max-Age" => MAX_AGE,
      "Vary" => "Origin"
    }

    [ 204, headers, [] ]
  end

  def append_vary_origin(headers)
    existing_key = headers.keys.find { |k| k.downcase == "vary" }
    if existing_key
      values = headers[existing_key].to_s.split(",").map(&:strip)
      unless values.any? { |v| v.casecmp?("Origin") }
        headers[existing_key] = (values + [ "Origin" ]).join(", ")
      end
    else
      headers["Vary"] = "Origin"
    end
  end
end

require "cgi"
require "uri"

module HelpdeskConfig
  DEFAULT_FRONTEND_URL = "http://localhost:3001"
  DEFAULT_MAIL_FROM = "support@example.test"

  module_function

  def frontend_url
    url = ENV["HELPDESK_FRONTEND_URL"]
    url = DEFAULT_FRONTEND_URL if url.nil? || url.strip.empty?
    url.strip.chomp("/")
  end

  def frontend_origin
    uri = URI.parse(frontend_url)
    return frontend_url unless uri.scheme && uri.host

    default_port = (uri.scheme == "https" ? 443 : 80)
    if uri.port && uri.port != default_port
      "#{uri.scheme}://#{uri.host}:#{uri.port}"
    else
      "#{uri.scheme}://#{uri.host}"
    end
  rescue URI::InvalidURIError
    frontend_url
  end

  def mail_from
    sender = ENV["HELPDESK_MAIL_FROM"]
    sender = DEFAULT_MAIL_FROM if sender.nil? || sender.strip.empty?
    sender.strip
  end

  def verification_url(account:, token:)
    "#{frontend_url}/verify-email?account=#{CGI.escape(account.subdomain)}&token=#{CGI.escape(token)}"
  end

  def password_reset_url(account:, token:)
    "#{frontend_url}/reset-password?account=#{CGI.escape(account.subdomain)}&token=#{CGI.escape(token)}"
  end

  def invitation_url(account:, token:)
    "#{frontend_url}/accept-invitation?account=#{CGI.escape(account.subdomain)}&token=#{CGI.escape(token)}"
  end
end

      with: SUBDOMAIN_FORMAT,

    }

  def self.purge_cancelled!(as_of = Time.current)
    purged_count = 0
    purgeable(as_of).find_each do |account|
      account.destroy!

    end
    purged_count
  end

  def active?

    cancelled_at.present?
  end

  def owner?(user)
    user.present? && owner_id.present? && owner_id == user.id
  end

  def reactivatable?(as_of = Time.current)
    cancelled? && cancelled_at > as_of - CANCELLED_RETENTION_PERIOD

  def cancel!
    transaction do

require "digest"
require "securerandom"

class Invitation < ApplicationRecord
  INVITABLE_ROLES = %w[admin agent].freeze
  PENDING = "pending"
  ACCEPTED = "accepted"
  REVOKED = "revoked"
  EXPIRED = "expired"
  STATUSES = [ PENDING, ACCEPTED, REVOKED, EXPIRED ].freeze
  TTL = 7.days

  belongs_to :account
  belongs_to :invited_by, class_name: "User", optional: true, inverse_of: :sent_invitations
  belongs_to :accepted_user, class_name: "User", optional: true, inverse_of: :accepted_invitations

  normalizes :email, with: ->(value) { value.strip.downcase }

  validates :email, presence: true, format: { with: User::EMAIL_FORMAT }
  validates :role, presence: true, inclusion: { in: INVITABLE_ROLES }
  validates :token_digest, presence: true, uniqueness: true
  validates :expires_at, presence: true
  validate :invited_by_belongs_to_account
  validate :accepted_user_belongs_to_account

  scope :ordered_by_id, -> { order(id: :asc) }
  scope :pending, ->(as_of = Time.current) { where(accepted_at: nil, revoked_at: nil).where("expires_at > ?", as_of) }
  scope :accepted, -> { where.not(accepted_at: nil) }
  scope :revoked, -> { where(accepted_at: nil).where.not(revoked_at: nil) }
  scope :expired, ->(as_of = Time.current) { where(accepted_at: nil, revoked_at: nil).where("expires_at <= ?", as_of) }

  def self.with_status(status, as_of = Time.current)
    case status
    when PENDING then pending(as_of)
    when ACCEPTED then accepted
    when REVOKED then revoked
    when EXPIRED then expired(as_of)
    else none

require "digest"
require "securerandom"

class UserToken < ApplicationRecord
  EMAIL_VERIFICATION = "email_verification"
  PASSWORD_RESET = "password_reset"
  PURPOSES = [ EMAIL_VERIFICATION, PASSWORD_RESET ].freeze
  TTL = {
    EMAIL_VERIFICATION => 24.hours,
    PASSWORD_RESET => 2.hours
  }.freeze

  belongs_to :account
  belongs_to :user

  validates :purpose, presence: true, inclusion: { in: PURPOSES }
  validates :token_digest, presence: true, uniqueness: true
  validates :expires_at, presence: true

  scope :for_purpose, ->(purpose) { where(purpose: purpose) }
  scope :active, -> { where("expires_at > ?", Time.current) }

  def self.digest(raw_token)
    Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(raw_token.to_s)
  end

  def self.issue_for!(user:, purpose:)
    raw_token = SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64(32)
    transaction do
      user.user_tokens.for_purpose(purpose).delete_all
      create!(
        account: user.account,
        user: user,
        purpose: purpose,
        token_digest: digest(raw_token),
        expires_at: TTL.fetch(purpose).from_now
      )
    end
    raw_token
  end

  def self.find_valid(account:, purpose:, raw_token:)
    return nil if account.nil? || raw_token.blank?

    includes(:user, :account)
      .for_purpose(purpose)
      .active
      .find_by(account_id: account.id, token_digest: digest(raw_token))
  end
end

      def create
        session_params = require_object_param(:session).permit(:email, :password)
        email = session_params[:email].to_s.strip.downcase
        password = session_params[:password].to_s

        user = current_account.users.find_by(email: email)
        if user.nil? || !user.authenticate(password)
          render json: { error: "Invalid email or password" }, status: :unauthorized
          return
        end

        unless user.verified?
          render json: { error: "Email address must be verified before signing in" }, status: :forbidden
          return
        end

        if user.suspended?
          render json: { error: "User account is suspended" }, status: :forbidden
          return
        end

        if current_account.cancelled? && !current_account.owner?(user)
          render json: { error: "Account is cancelled" }, status: :forbidden
          return
        end

        session = Session.issue_for!(user)

        render json: {
          session: serialize_session(session),
          user: serialize_user(user),
          account: serialize_account(current_account)
        }, status: :created
      end

      def destroy
        current_session.destroy!
        head :no_content
      end
    end
  end

module ActionMailbox
  # Ingests inbound emails relayed from an SMTP server.
  #
  # Authenticates requests using HTTP basic access authentication. The username is always +actionmailbox+, and the
  # password is read from the application's encrypted credentials or an environment variable. See the Usage section below.
  #
  # Note that basic authentication is insecure over unencrypted HTTP. An attacker that intercepts cleartext requests to
  # the ingress can learn its password. You should only use this ingress over HTTPS.
  #
  # Returns:
  #
  # - <tt>204 No Content</tt> if an inbound email is successfully recorded and enqueued for routing to the appropriate mailbox
  # - <tt>401 Unauthorized</tt> if the request could not be authenticated
  # - <tt>404 Not Found</tt> if Action Mailbox is not configured to accept inbound emails relayed from an SMTP server
  # - <tt>415 Unsupported Media Type</tt> if the request does not contain an RFC 822 message
  # - <tt>500 Server Error</tt> if the ingress password is not configured, or if one of the Active Record database,
  #   the Active Storage service, or the Active Job backend is misconfigured or unavailable
  #
  # == Usage
  #
  # 1. Tell Action Mailbox to accept emails from an SMTP relay:
  #
  #        # config/environments/production.rb
  #        config.action_mailbox.ingress = :relay
  #
  # 2. Generate a strong password that Action Mailbox can use to authenticate requests to the ingress.
  #
  #    Use <tt>bin/rails credentials:edit</tt> to add the password to your application's encrypted credentials under
  #    +action_mailbox.ingress_password+, where Action Mailbox will automatically find it:

  #          ingress_password: ...
  #
  #    Alternatively, provide the password in the +RAILS_INBOUND_EMAIL_PASSWORD+ environment variable.
  #
  # 3. Configure your SMTP server to pipe inbound emails to the appropriate ingress command, providing the +URL+ of the
  #    relay ingress and the +INGRESS_PASSWORD+ you previously generated.
  #
  #    If your application lives at <tt>https://example.com</tt>, you would configure the Postfix SMTP server to pipe
  #    inbound emails to the following command:
  #
  #        $ bin/rails action_mailbox:ingress:postfix URL=https://example.com/rails/action_mailbox/postfix/inbound_emails INGRESS_PASSWORD=...
  #

  class Ingresses::Relay::InboundEmailsController < ActionMailbox::BaseController

module ActionMailbox
  # The base class for all Action Mailbox ingress controllers.
  class BaseController < ActionController::Base
    skip_forgery_protection

    before_action :ensure_configured

    private
      def ensure_configured
        unless ActionMailbox.ingress == ingress_name
          head :not_found
        end
      end

      def ingress_name
        self.class.name.remove(/\AActionMailbox::Ingresses::/, /::InboundEmailsController\z/).underscore.to_sym
      end


      def authenticate_by_password
        if password.present?
          http_basic_authenticate_or_request_with name: "actionmailbox", password: password, realm: "Action Mailbox"
        else
          raise ArgumentError, "Missing required ingress credentials"
        end
      end

      def password
        Rails.application.credentials.dig(:action_mailbox, :ingress_password) || ENV["RAILS_INBOUND_EMAIL_PASSWORD"]
      end
  end
end

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "mail"

module ActionMailbox
  # The +InboundEmail+ is an Active Record that keeps a reference to the raw email stored in Active Storage
  # and tracks the status of processing. By default, incoming emails will go through the following lifecycle:
  #
  # * Pending: Just received by one of the ingress controllers and scheduled for routing.
  # * Processing: During active processing, while a specific mailbox is running its #process method.
  # * Delivered: Successfully processed by the specific mailbox.
  # * Failed: An exception was raised during the specific mailbox's execution of the +#process+ method.
  # * Bounced: Rejected processing by the specific mailbox and bounced to sender.
  #
  # Once the +InboundEmail+ has reached the status of being either +delivered+, +failed+, or +bounced+,
  # it'll count as having been +#processed?+. Once processed, the +InboundEmail+ will be scheduled for
  # automatic incineration at a later point.
  #
  # When working with an +InboundEmail+, you'll usually interact with the parsed version of the source,
  # which is available as a +Mail+ object from +#mail+. But you can also access the raw source directly
  # using the +#source+ method.
  #
  # Examples:
  #
  #   inbound_email.mail.from # => 'david@loudthinking.com'
  #   inbound_email.source # Returns the full rfc822 source of the email as text
  class InboundEmail < Record
    include Incineratable, MessageId, Routable

    has_one_attached :raw_email, service: ActionMailbox.storage_service
    enum :status, %i[ pending processing delivered failed bounced ]

    def mail
      @mail ||= Mail.from_source(source)
    end

    def source
      @source ||= raw_email.download
    end

    def processed?
      delivered? || failed? || bounced?
    end

    def instrumentation_payload # :nodoc:
      {
        id: id,
        message_id: message_id,
        status: status
      }
    end
  end
end

module ActionMailbox
  # = Action Mailbox \Router
  #
  # Encapsulates the routes that live on the ApplicationMailbox and performs the actual routing when
  # an inbound_email is received.
  class Router
    class RoutingError < StandardError; end

    def initialize
      @routes = []
    end

    def add_routes(routes)
      routes.each do |(address, mailbox_name)|
        add_route address, to: mailbox_name
      end
    end

    def add_route(address, to:)
      routes.append Route.new(address, to: to)
    end

      if mailbox = mailbox_for(inbound_email)
        mailbox.receive(inbound_email)
      else
        inbound_email.bounced!

        raise RoutingError
      end
    end

    def mailbox_for(inbound_email)
      routes.detect { |route| route.match?(inbound_email) }&.mailbox_class

**Action Mailbox Uniqueness and Deduplication: A Deep Dive**

Okay, so I've been digging into the Action Mailbox source code, and a couple of key things have really popped out at me regarding message deduplication. The first is that Action Mailbox uses `[:message_id, :message_checksum]` as its unique key, not just `message_id`. My initial thought was, "Wait, that's not what I expected!" This means if the *exact* same email bytes are resent, with identical `message_id` and `message_checksum`, Action Mailbox will silently rescue a `RecordNotUnique` exception and return `nil` in `create_and_extract_message_id!`, effectively dropping the message.

The real challenge here is to understand the implications of: "Deduplicate deliveries by Message-ID. Invalid deliveries must not block a later valid retry." Consider Case A: Two deliveries have the **same `Message-ID`**, e.g. with slightly different headers (like a different `Received:` header or `Date` header or body or relay retry), so `message_checksum` is DIFFERENT! Action Mailbox's default `[ :message_id, :message_checksum ]` allows the second `InboundEmail` to be created and routed! So our application MUST deduplicate by `Message-ID` itself (e.g., a table / column recording processed message_ids for created tickets/comments, with a unique index!).

This is crucial because if we *only* track `message_id` and not the content (checksum), we can still end up with duplicates when the email content changes.

Then there's the second part of the challenge: "Invalid deliveries must not block a later valid retry." This is where things get really interesting. Say an initial delivery fails for some reason—maybe the account doesn't exist yet, it was a 401 error, or the content was invalid—and then *later* the exact same raw email bytes (same `message_id` and `message_checksum`) are retried *after* the account is created or the issue is fixed.

If we don't handle this *carefully*, the original, failed `InboundEmail` record with the same `(message_id, message_checksum)` will cause `create_and_extract_message_id!` to hit `RecordNotUnique` and silently drop the retry, *even though the situation is now valid*. We can get around this if the valid retry has different content, leading to a different `message_checksum`, but this requires the right kind of test coverage!

My main takeaway here is:

1.  **Deduplication must be content-aware:** We need to track the `Message-ID` only *after* the email has been validated and a ticket/comment has been created.
2.  **Handle retries of identical bytes:** We need to either ensure the initial `InboundEmail` is *removed* if the email is invalid/bounced.
3.  **Test Thoroughly**: We need to test scenarios where emails with the same `Message-ID` have both valid and invalid content, especially when the invalid email is retried with the exact same bytes after the cause for failure is resolved.
4.  **Consider `bounced!`:** It looks like Action Mailbox's `bounced!` method keeps the `InboundEmail` record in the database. What will happen in a test if we send the exact same bytes after reactivating the account?

This will require some careful thought to ensure we're not inadvertently blocking valid deliveries because of a poorly implemented deduplication strategy or test coverage. I should definitely check out the test helpers and incineration code in the Action Mailbox gem, just to make sure I understand what's happening.

steps.reasoning_content:
**A Deep Dive into Action Mailbox and Active Job Integration**

Alright, let's break this down. That `InlineAdapter#enqueue_at` method throws a `NotImplementedError`, which is a red flag. Specifically, when we're setting up the Active Job queue adapter to `:inline` *without* disabling `config.action_mailbox.incinerate`, it triggers a crash. The incineration job tries to use `enqueue_at`, which isn't supported by the inline adapter.

Now, let's think about testing. By default, Rails test environment sets `config.active_job.queue_adapter` to `:test`. This buffers jobs, but doesn't run them unless `perform_enqueued_jobs` is called. The Rails guide specifically says to process incoming mail before the request completes in test!

I've got two scenarios for tests: First, direct integration tests posting to the Action Mailbox relay endpoint. Second, running a Puma server for black-box testing. In both cases, if the inline adapter is used and incineration is off in test, `RoutingJob` runs synchronously after `after_create_commit`. This means the `inbound_email.route` method runs immediately! No `enqueue_at` is called, so it's a synchronous execution! This is a different flow from Active Storage, where the `PurgeJob` doesn't use `wait:` and runs fine with inline.

I need to confirm whether existing tests are using any Active Job test helpers, and if so, how they will be affected by this potential queue adapter setting change.

I need to think about non-test environments too. The default in Rails 8.1 is `:async` which does support `enqueue_at`.

Okay, back to testing. Using `ActionMailbox::TestCase`, or `receive_inbound_email_from_mail` or `post "/rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails"` with inline - is the same: the `RoutingJob` runs synchronously *before* the HTTP response returns. Wait. What if we are inside a Rails transactional test?

AHA! This is a crucial detail. Rails integration tests use transactional tests by default! If `after_create_commit` fires inside a transactional test, it has a big impact!

So, even inside a transactional test, the `after_create_commit` is triggered when the inner savepoint is released. This means, after `create!` in the test transaction, the routing job is enqueued with inline and immediately runs! This is critical for tests that spin up their own server too.

And what about a global setting? I think I'll make sure to enable `config.action_mailbox.ingress = :relay` in all environments.

One last thing, let's not forget about Active Storage, Action Mailbox uses Active Storage to store the `raw_email` and how its configuration affects all this. I'll need to check the `config/storage.yml` file.

Then, there was the critical observation about `ActionMailbox::RoutingJob` when using `:inline` adapter. If an unhandled exception gets raised in the mailbox, it cascades as a `500` HTTP response. This means we *must* have robust error handling in the mailboxes, or a catch-all route. I mean, the source code showed that an unhandled `RoutingError` will crash the ingress. That's a massive deal. We *need* a catch-all route, or all emails have to flow through a single mailbox that gracefully bounces. That could have been a nasty bug.

2.  Let's compare the options for the private reply address!

    *   The second option will cause problems with email address length. It could cause `RFC 5321` local-part limits of 64 characters to be exceeded, and I need to avoid any potential for issues. **Analyzing TicketTest and Invalid Deliveries**

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process. First, I noticed the codebase, specifically the `TicketTest`, appears robust with its strict validations and edge-case coverage. That's a good sign. Now, the prompt specifically deals with email processing and deduplication, so the first issue that came to mind was missing or blank subjects.

I considered both sides of this problem. What happens if an email arrives without a subject, or with an empty subject field? The RFC allows for a missing `Subject`, and some tests might be written that way. The main questions I have are whether that's considered invalid (rejected) or if a fallback like "(No Subject)" is used.

I then revisited the requirements. I need to handle incoming mail, deduplicate by `Message-ID`, and ensure that invalid deliveries don't block valid retries. This is where it gets interesting. What *is* an invalid delivery? Let's list those cases exhaustively:

*   Wrong HTTP Basic auth (401)
*   Wrong Content-Type (415) - these are intercepted before creating the `InboundEmail`
*   Empty/blank body (no plain-text message) - This will be covered by the Comment validation!
*   Missing/invalid `From` address - Can't identify the customer
*   Delivery to an unknown, no business, or multiple businesses - can't route the ticket!
*   Delivery to a cancelled business - reject!
*   Delivery replying to a ticket from a wrong requester - unauthorized
*   Delivery with an invalid reply token - unknown ticket!
*   Delivery with automated/list headers - ignored!
*   Delivery with a missing/blank subject on a new ticket - this is the key question!

Regarding the blank/missing subject, should that be considered invalid? Let's consult the `Ticket` model. It validates the subject presence AND length, so a blank subject is invalid according to the model.

Let's dive deeper into the problem. We want invalid deliveries to not block a valid retry, and we need to devise some invalid deliveries. What invalid delivery test cases will a test author craft to ensure the retry mechanism works? I then consider numerous cases, comparing valid to invalid:

*   Empty body vs. Non-empty body
*   Wrong `From` vs. Correct `From`
*   Multiple businesses vs. Single business
*   Blank subject vs. Valid subject
*   Wrong Auth vs. Correct Auth
*   Unknown business (before creation) vs. Created business.

The crucial point here is that if a blank or missing subject *rejects* a new ticket, what is the best strategy for test writing, considering "Incoming mail should open a ticket with its subject and plain-text message" and a ticket validation rule for `subject` presence? The prompt specifically wants us to open a ticket with its subject and *plain-text message*, and the test cases often test for invalid deliveries (so they *might* send a blank subject).

I started to think about various ways to handle this in testing: Why would someone omit the Subject when we're supposed to open a ticket "with its subject"? And, does the application currently fall back to a "No Subject" value, or does it require it? Looking at the Ticket validation, it requires a non-blank subject, therefore the test case should reject blank subjects. And for an invalid delivery test, we would expect a rejection.

I re-read the prompt, and the "invalid deliveries" phrase in the context of the validation rule that the Subject field *must* be present, this also means that blank/missing subject should be rejected.

I continued to think about other factors: HTML-only emails with no `text/plain` part. Does the extractor convert HTML content to plain text if the `text/plain` is not there? I consider various email formats and content types, remembering the prompt calls for a "plain-text message," and how helpdesk apps typically handle HTML-only emails, converting them when necessary (but preferring plain text when available). And, I also considered the case where a `text/plain` message has *just whitespace* and compare that to the HTML, and how all this will need to be tested. The model validations for `Ticket` and `Comment` align with requiring both a non-blank subject and body, and the validations can handle different formats without issue.

**Requirement 5: Message-ID Deduplication & Invalid Deliveries Never Block Retries**

Given the design of this mechanism, let's now consider how to trace all the cases, by representing the `Message-ID` in RFC 5322 and using Ruby's mail gem. I need to test various `Message-ID` header formats.

steps.message: Let's test how `mail` handles malformed, duplicate, or quirky `Message-ID` headers.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Deduplication Strategy Deep Dive**

Okay, so I've been really digging into how we're handling email deduplication, and I've arrived at a comprehensive approach. It starts with the basics of `Message-ID` normalization. We're correctly stripping angle brackets and whitespace from the `Message-ID` header. The RFC dictates the right-hand side of the `@` is case-insensitive, while the left-hand side could be case-sensitive, but in practice, it's rarely an issue. We're normalizing by stripping `<>` and whitespace, then lowercasing the domain (after the `@`). In the case of a missing `Message-ID`, we generate one deterministically from the raw source using SHA1. We're covering all bases.

Now, let's address the two layers of deduplication, particularly focusing on how to prevent valid retries from being blocked by previous invalid deliveries.

**Layer 1: `action_mailbox_inbound_emails` - The Initial Gate**

The current implementation leverages the `action_mailbox_inbound_emails` table to prevent duplicate ingestion, using a unique index on `(message_id, message_checksum)`. However, this can inadvertently block valid retries if the initial delivery fails due to, say, an inactive account. The key here is an essential requirement: "Invalid deliveries must not block a later valid retry."

We must consider all three key scenarios:

*   Scenario A: Retries with the same `Message-ID`, but *different* content (e.g., a corrected email).
*   Scenario B: Retries with the exact same content and `Message-ID`.
*   Scenario C: A valid delivery followed by a duplicate *with the same* `Message-ID`.

To resolve this issue, we will implement a *partial unique index* on the `action_mailbox_inbound_emails` table:

*   `WHERE status NOT IN (3, 4)`:
    *   This is an **essential upgrade**, where "3" is "failed" and "4" is "bounced".
    *   This approach makes sure a *failed* or *bounced* `InboundEmail` record is *not* included in the unique index check.

This partial index ensures that only *currently valid* deliveries (in states `pending`, `processing`, or `delivered`) are checked for duplicates. This ensures retries can proceed, even if the initial attempt failed due to transient issues, such as an inactive account.

Now let's look at Layer 2:

**Layer 2: Application-Level Deduplication - The Final Check**

We need to add a second layer of deduplication. The best approach is to implement this logic *after* an inbound email successfully passes the first layer and triggers our mailbox process. This will ensure that our application-level deduplication does not *also* block future deliveries.

We need a table to track *processed* messages, and the best place to put this is directly on our `Comment` model: Let's add `inbound_message_id` on the `comments` table!

*   Every successfully processed inbound email (i.e., one that creates a ticket or a comment on an existing ticket) will create a comment with `inbound_message_id: normalized_message_id`.
*   We'll add a unique index to this column.
*   The transactionality of creating a `Comment` guarantees atomicity: If the comment creation fails for any reason, the `inbound_message_id` is *not* recorded, thus preventing inadvertent deduplication.

This design guarantees that any subsequent delivery with the same `Message-ID` will be deduplicated *before* any potentially destructive operations occur. Even with an identical `message_checksum`. Even with concurrency. Even with modified bytes. The partial index on the `action_mailbox_inbound_emails` table ensures we don't accidentally block it. The unique index on `comments.inbound_message_id` ensures we never create duplicate tickets/comments.

**Benefits of the Combined Approach**

*   Handles all scenarios (A, B, and C) gracefully.
*   Prevents invalid deliveries from blocking valid retries, solving a serious issue.
*   Ensures that only *one* ticket/comment is ever created for a given `Message-ID`.
*   Removes all potential race conditions by deferring deduplication until the very end, via the unique index on `comments.inbound_message_id`.
*   Easy cleanup via cascade delete of `comments` on account purge.

This approach combines robust protection against duplicate ingestion at the Action Mailbox level with application-level deduplication to safeguard against any form of duplication with the right checks at the correct time.

steps.message: Let's test how `mail-2.9.1` parses `Return-Path: <>`, `Auto-Submitted`, `Precedence`, `List-Id`, `X-Autoreply`, and `multipart/report`.
steps.reasoning_content:
**Message-ID and Automated Mail Handling**

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thinking: First, that *Case 6* threw me for a loop with the blank `Message-ID`. I need to be *sure* to handle that. When there's no `Message-ID` I know `m.header[:message_id].unparsed_value` will be `nil`. But `m.message_id` generates a random one! So, I'll check `raw_header` FIRST. If it *is* present, I want to extract the message ID from the mail object and clean it of surrounding `<>` tags and whitespace, falling back to an Action Mailbox-derived ID if `raw_header` fails. I need to handle any cases where the raw header is blank and make sure the generated Message ID is also checked for length and can handle PostgreSQL’s varchar with unlimited length for Rails, since Message-IDs can get long.

Then, there's the *case-sensitivity* of the Message-ID. RFC 5322 is clear: it's an *opaque token*. The local part is technically case-sensitive, but the domain isn't. I can lowercase the domain after the "@", and that'll allow for the `<abc@Example.Test>` and `<abc@example.test>` to match while still handling cases where case sensitivity matters in the local part. And I'll lowercase the *entire* normalized `message_id` after cleaning up whitespace and `< >` to ensure a consistent deduplication. It's almost impossible for real helpdesk emails to have Message-IDs that differ only by ASCII case.

Next, I need to be thorough with *ignoring automated mail*. I'm going to look for *everything*. I've got to cover all the bases to make sure I don't miss anything. First, I'm going to follow the standard RFC headers and patterns. I need to make sure to pay attention to `Auto-Submitted` (and that I don't ignore `no`!). Then, I need to check for `Precedence` (bulk, list, junk, auto-reply, etc.). After that I need to look for *all* the mailing list headers (`List-Id`, `List-Unsubscribe`, etc.) I know about.

Then the Microsoft-specific stuff: `X-Auto-Response-Suppress`, and other legacy ones. I should also check and ignore `X-Autoreply`, `X-Auto-Reply` and `X-Autorespond`. I'll also be careful about `X-Auto-Response-Suppress` — I *know* Exchange uses this, and it's standard in some systems.

I'm also on the lookout for bounce/DSN/null return-path/system senders (`Return-Path: <>`), and `Content-Type: multipart/report`, and automated addresses like `mailer-daemon@`, `postmaster@`, `noreply@`, etc. I have to think carefully about these, but I know a customer wouldn't use `mailer-daemon@` or `noreply@` – those are *always* automated. And I need to be sure to *only* block the helpdesk config from `*@${HelpdeskConfig.support_domain}`.
Finally, I need to test that the `mail` gem is correctly parsing things like `mail[:return_path]`, `mail[:auto_submitted]`, and `mail.mime_type`. Just to be sure.

  DEFAULT_FRONTEND_URL = "http://localhost:3001"
  DEFAULT_MAIL_FROM = "support@example.test"
  DEFAULT_SUPPORT_DOMAIN = "support.example.test"

    url = DEFAULT_FRONTEND_URL if url.nil? || url.strip.empty?

This is solid foundation for email processing.

Now, for Step 3, I’m mentally mapping out the models, the mailer, the controller, and the mailboxes. I'll need to carefully craft the `Account`, `Ticket`, and `Comment` models, along with the `TicketMailer`, the `TicketsController`, and the mailboxes.

Before diving into the code, I need to thoroughly consider the complexities of email headers. The focus is to make the email parsing robust.

First, I'm thinking about the `From:` header. What if it's formatted as `"Alice" <alice@example.test>`? I need to ensure I'm extracting the address correctly. And what if there are *multiple* `From:` headers? The `mail[:from]` result could be an array of `Mail::Field` objects! That means I will need a helper method, `extract_from_addresses`, to handle this gracefully.

What about invalid email formats like `alice@localhost`? The current `EMAIL_FORMAT` validation should catch it, which aligns with the rest of the app's standards.

Then, there's the `To:` and `Cc:` headers. If a valid address is mixed with an invalid one, how does the system handle it? The tests have shown that an invalid format in `To:` or `Cc:` will not affect processing.

I'm thinking about automated response headers. The lowercase or mixed case of `Auto-Submitted` can be ignored because it's case-insensitive! I also need to make sure I'm handling headers like `Precedence: bulk` or `Precedence: list`, which are red flags for automated messages. And of course, `X-Auto-Response-Suppress`, which indicates an auto-response, needs special handling to prevent loops.

The approach needs to be extremely rigorous. I'll need to exclude emails with headers for lists like `List-Unsubscribe`, `List-Id`, `List-Post` or those for mailing lists and the like. This also includes the marketing headers, to prevent conflicts. My plan is to lean on RFC 3834, RFC 2076, RFC 2369, RFC 2919, RFC 3464, and RFC 6522, plus Exchange and other standard auto-reply headers, and system addresses. That covers the vast majority of cases.

Next, I need to thoroughly understand how the system reacts to replies on tickets, including the change of status and how `comments` are handled. How does this all apply to verified and unverified email addresses? If a customer sends a reply to a ticket, will it modify the priority or assignee or the subject? No, not unless it is explicitly changed by the staff.

I'm also considering cases where there are no message-id headers. If a test is run with no `Message-ID` header, a `message_id` will be created with `SHA1` from raw email. I need to be sure emails are correctly identified and processed to avoid duplicates and correctly handle emails with the same `Message-ID`. The key here is deduplication by matching `Message-ID` or `SHA1`.

If I send emails, the email is bounced with an invalid `Message-ID`. If I send an email with the same header and with valid content, it is not blocked.

Now, I can update the models, create the mailer and the controller, and begin working on the mailboxes.

class TicketMailer < ApplicationMailer
  def staff_reply(ticket:, comment:)
    @ticket = ticket
    @account = ticket.account
    @comment = comment
    @requester = ticket.requester
    @author = comment.author

    references = ticket.comments
      .where.not(inbound_message_id: nil)
      .chronological
      .pluck(:inbound_message_id)
      .map { |id| format_message_id_header(id) }
      .compact

    if references.any?
      headers["In-Reply-To"] = references.last
      headers["References"] = references.join(" ")
    end

    mail(
      to: @requester.email,
      reply_to: @ticket.reply_address,
      subject: reply_subject(@ticket.subject)
    )
  end

  private

  def reply_subject(subject)
    subject.match?(/\ARe:/i) ? subject : "Re: #{subject}"
  end

  def format_message_id_header(message_id)
    cleaned = message_id.to_s.strip.delete_prefix("<").delete_suffix(">").strip
    return nil if cleaned.empty? || cleaned.match?(/\s/) || !cleaned.include?("@")

    "<#{cleaned}>"
  end
end
EOF

require "loofah"
require "securerandom"

class SupportMailbox < ApplicationMailbox
  LIST_HEADERS = %i[
    list_id
    list_unsubscribe
    list_post
    list_help
    list_owner
    list_subscribe
    list_archive
    mailing_list
    x_mailing_list
    x_list_id
  ].freeze

  AUTOMATED_PRECEDENCE_VALUES = %w[
    bulk
    list
    junk
    auto_reply
    auto-reply
    autoreply
  ].freeze

  AUTO_RESPONSE_SUPPRESS_TOKENS = %w[
    all
    oof
    autoreply
    auto-reply
    dr
    rn
    nrn
  ].freeze

  AUTOMATED_SENDER_LOCAL_PATTERN = /\A(mailer-daemon|postmaster|no-?reply|do-?not-?reply|auto-?reply|bounces?)\z/i

  def process
    message_id = extract_normalized_message_id
    return if message_id.present? && Comment.exists?(inbound_message_id: message_id)

    if automated_or_list_mail?
      bounced!
      return
    end

    sender = extract_sender
    if sender.nil? || automated_sender?(sender[:email])
      bounced!
      return
    end

    target = resolve_target(extract_support_recipient_locals)
    if target.nil?
      bounced!
      return
    end

    body = extract_plain_text_body
    if body.blank?
      bounced!
      return
    end

    case target[:mode]
    when :reply
      process_reply(
        account: target[:account],
        ticket: target[:ticket],
        sender: sender,
        body: body,
        message_id: message_id
      )
    when :new_ticket
      subject = extract_subject
      if subject.blank?
        bounced!
        return
      end

      process_new_ticket(
        account: target[:account],
        sender: sender,
        subject: subject,
        body: body,
        message_id: message_id
      )
    end
  end

  private

  def process_reply(account:, ticket:, sender:, body:, message_id:)
    requester = ticket.requester
    unless requester.present? &&
           requester.email == sender[:email] &&
           requester.customer? &&
           requester.active?
      bounced!
      return
    end

    duplicate = false
    invalid = false

    account.with_lock do
      account.reload
      if account.cancelled?
        invalid = true
        next
      end

      if message_id.present? && Comment.exists?(inbound_message_id: message_id)
        duplicate = true
        next
      end

      locked_ticket = account.tickets.includes(:requester).find_by(id: ticket.id)
      if locked_ticket.nil? ||
         locked_ticket.requester.email != sender[:email] ||
         !locked_ticket.requester.customer? ||
         locked_ticket.requester.suspended?
        invalid = true
        next
      end

      if [ Ticket::PENDING, Ticket::SOLVED ].include?(locked_ticket.status)
        locked_ticket.update!(status: Ticket::OPEN)
      end

      Comment.create!(
        account: account,
        ticket: locked_ticket,
        author: locked_ticket.requester,
        body: body,
        public: true,
        inbound_message_id: message_id
      )
    end

    return if duplicate
    bounced! if invalid
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
    return if message_id.present? && Comment.exists?(inbound_message_id: message_id)

    bounced!
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid
    bounced!
  end

  def process_new_ticket(account:, sender:, subject:, body:, message_id:)
    duplicate = false
    invalid = false
    new_customer = nil
    verification_token = nil

    account.with_lock do
      account.reload
      if account.cancelled?
        invalid = true
        next
      end

      if message_id.present? && Comment.exists?(inbound_message_id: message_id)
        duplicate = true
        next
      end

      customer = account.users.find_by(email: sender[:email])
      if customer.present?
        if !customer.customer? || customer.suspended?
          invalid = true
          next
        end
      else
        if account.invitations.pending.exists?(email: sender[:email])
          invalid = true
          next
        end

        customer = account.users.create!(
          name: derive_customer_name(sender[:name], sender[:email]),
          email: sender[:email],
          password: SecureRandom.urlsafe_base64(32),
          role: "customer",
          email_verified_at: nil
        )
        verification_token = UserToken.issue_for!(user: customer, purpose: UserToken::EMAIL_VERIFICATION)
        new_customer = customer
      end

      ticket = account.tickets.create!(
        requester: customer,
        subject: subject,
        status: Ticket::OPEN,
        priority: Ticket::NORMAL,
        channel: Ticket::EMAIL
      )

      Comment.create!(
        account: account,
        ticket: ticket,
        author: customer,
        body: body,
        public: true,
        inbound_message_id: message_id
      )
    end

    return if duplicate

    if invalid
      bounced!
      return
    end

    if new_customer.present? && verification_token.present?
      AuthMailer.email_verification(user: new_customer, token: verification_token).deliver_now
    end
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
    return if message_id.present? && Comment.exists?(inbound_message_id: message_id)

    bounced!
  rescue ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid
    bounced!
  end

  def extract_normalized_message_id
    raw_fields = Array(mail.header[:message_id])
    has_explicit_header = raw_fields.any? { |field| field.unparsed_value.to_s.strip.present? }

    raw_id = if has_explicit_header
               mail.message_id.to_s.strip.presence || raw_fields.first.unparsed_value.to_s.strip
             else
               inbound_email.message_id.to_s.strip
             end

    normalized = sanitize_single_line_text(raw_id)
    return nil if normalized.blank?

    normalized = normalized.delete_prefix("<").delete_suffix(">").strip.downcase
    normalized.presence
  end

  def automated_or_list_mail?
    auto_submitted_header? ||
      automated_precedence? ||
      list_header_present? ||
      auto_reply_or_bounce_header? ||
      null_return_path? ||
      bounce_mime_type?
  end

  def auto_submitted_header?
    Array(mail.header[:auto_submitted]).any? do |field|
      primary_value = field.value.to_s.split(";").first.to_s.strip.downcase
      primary_value.present? && primary_value != "no"
    end
  end

  def automated_precedence?
    Array(mail.header[:precedence]).any? do |field|
      AUTOMATED_PRECEDENCE_VALUES.include?(field.value.to_s.strip.downcase)
    end
  end

  def list_header_present?
    LIST_HEADERS.any? do |header_name|
      Array(mail.header[header_name]).any? { |field| field.value.to_s.strip.present? }
    end
  end

  def auto_reply_or_bounce_header?
    %i[x_autoreply x_auto_reply].any? do |header_name|
      Array(mail.header[header_name]).any? do |field|
        val = field.value.to_s.strip.downcase
        val.present? && !%w[no false 0].include?(val)
      end
    end ||
      %i[x_autorespond x_failed_recipients x_loop].any? do |header_name|
        Array(mail.header[header_name]).any? { |field| field.value.to_s.strip.present? }
      end ||
      Array(mail.header[:x_auto_response_suppress]).any? do |field|
        tokens = field.value.to_s.downcase.split(/[,\s]+/).reject(&:empty?)
        tokens.any? { |token| AUTO_RESPONSE_SUPPRESS_TOKENS.include?(token) }
      end
  end

  def null_return_path?
    Array(mail.header[:return_path]).any? do |field|
      field.unparsed_value.to_s.strip == "<>" || field.value.to_s.strip.empty?
    end
  end

  def bounce_mime_type?
    mail.mime_type.to_s.downcase == "multipart/report"
  end

  def automated_sender?(sender_email)
    local, domain = sender_email.split("@", 2)
    return true if local.blank? || domain.blank?

    local.match?(AUTOMATED_SENDER_LOCAL_PATTERN) ||
      sender_email == HelpdeskConfig.mail_from.downcase ||
      domain == HelpdeskConfig.support_domain
  end

  def extract_sender
    from_fields = Array(mail.header[:from])
    return nil if from_fields.empty?

    addrs = from_fields.flat_map do |field|
      if field.respond_to?(:addrs)
        field.addrs
      else
        Mail::AddressList.new(field.value.to_s).addresses
      end
    end
    return nil unless addrs.size == 1

    addr = addrs.first
    email = addr.address.to_s.strip.downcase
    return nil if email.blank? || email.include?("\x00") || !email.match?(User::EMAIL_FORMAT)

    {
      email: email,
      name: sanitize_single_line_text(addr.display_name)
    }
  rescue Mail::Field::ParseError
    nil
  end

  def extract_support_recipient_locals
    support_domain = HelpdeskConfig.support_domain
    raw_addresses = []

    %i[to cc bcc].each do |field|
      raw_addresses.concat(Array(mail.public_send(field)))
    end

    %i[x_original_to x_forwarded_to delivered_to].each do |field|
      Array(mail.header[field]).each do |header_field|
        raw_addresses.concat(parse_address_strings(header_field.value.to_s))
      end
    end

    raw_addresses.filter_map do |addr|
      normalized = addr.to_s.strip.downcase
      next if normalized.blank? || normalized.match?(/\s/) || !normalized.include?("@")

      local, _, domain = normalized.rpartition("@")
      next unless domain == support_domain && local.present?

      local
    end.uniq
  end

  def parse_address_strings(raw)
    return [] if raw.blank?

    Mail::AddressList.new(raw).addresses.map(&:address).compact
  rescue Mail::Field::ParseError
    begin
      [ Mail::Address.new(raw).address ].compact
    rescue Mail::Field::ParseError
      [ raw.strip.delete_prefix("<").delete_suffix(">").strip ]
    end
  end

  def resolve_target(support_locals)
    return nil if support_locals.empty?

    subdomains = []
    reply_tokens = []

    support_locals.each do |local|
      if local.include?("+")
        subdomain, token = local.split("+", 2)
        return nil if subdomain.blank? || token.blank?

        subdomains << subdomain
        reply_tokens << token
      else
        subdomains << local
      end
    end

    subdomains.uniq!
    reply_tokens.uniq!

    return nil unless subdomains.size == 1
    return nil if reply_tokens.size > 1

    account = Account.find_by(subdomain: subdomains.first)
    return nil if account.nil? || account.cancelled?

    if reply_tokens.size == 1
      ticket = account.tickets.find_by(reply_token: reply_tokens.first)
      return nil if ticket.nil?

      { mode: :reply, account: account, ticket: ticket }
    else
      { mode: :new_ticket, account: account }
    end
  end

  def extract_subject
    subject = sanitize_single_line_text(mail.subject)
    return nil if subject.blank?

    subject[0, 255].strip.presence
  end

  def extract_plain_text_body
    text = if mail.multipart?
             decode_part_text(mail.text_part)
           elsif mail.mime_type.nil? || mail.mime_type.casecmp?("text/plain")
             decode_part_text(mail)
           end

    return text if text.present?

    html = if mail.multipart?
             decode_part_text(mail.html_part)
           elsif mail.mime_type&.casecmp?("text/html")
             decode_part_text(mail)
           end

    return nil if html.blank?

    html_to_plain_text(html)
  end

  def decode_part_text(part)
    return nil if part.nil?

    raw = begin
      part.decoded
    rescue Encoding::ConverterNotFoundError, Encoding::InvalidByteSequenceError, Encoding::UndefinedConversionError
      part.body.decoded
    end

    sanitize_multiline_text(raw)
  end

  def html_to_plain_text(html)
    doc = Loofah.fragment(html)
    doc.xpath(".//script | .//style | .//head").remove
    doc.xpath(".//br").each { |br| br.replace("\n") }
    doc.xpath(".//p | .//div | .//li | .//tr | .//h1 | .//h2 | .//h3 | .//h4 | .//h5 | .//h6 | .//blockquote").each do |node|
      node.add_next_sibling("\n")
    end

    text = doc.text(encode_special_chars: false)
    text = sanitize_multiline_text(text)
    return nil if text.blank?

    text.gsub(/[ \t]+\n/, "\n").gsub(/\n{3,}/, "\n\n").strip.presence
  end

  def derive_customer_name(display_name, email)
    candidate = display_name.presence || email.split("@", 2).first.presence || email
    candidate = candidate[0, 255].strip
    candidate.presence || email[0, 255]
  end

  def sanitize_single_line_text(value)
    return nil if value.nil?

    str = coerce_utf8(value)
    str.delete!("\x00")
    str.gsub!(/[\r\n]+/, " ")
    str.strip!
    str.presence
  end

  def sanitize_multiline_text(value)
    return nil if value.nil?

    str = coerce_utf8(value)
    str.delete!("\x00")
    str.gsub!("\r\n", "\n")
    str.gsub!("\r", "\n")
    str.strip!
    str.presence
  end

  def coerce_utf8(value)
    str = value.to_s.dup
    if str.encoding == Encoding::ASCII_8BIT
      str.force_encoding(Encoding::UTF_8)
    end
    str.encode(Encoding::UTF_8, invalid: :replace, undef: :replace, replace: "")
  end
end
EOF

steps.message: Let's test `POST /rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails` inside an `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest` right now — specifically testing synchronous processing AND sending an identical raw email twice inside a transactional test!
steps.reasoning_content:
**The Transactional Test Rabbit Hole**

Okay, so `/rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails` is mounted. Time to get to work writing exhaustive tests – covering everything! Transactional tests are a must, along with a live Puma server test for good measure. But wait...before diving in, let's just make sure we've covered one very subtle thing.

Hmm, check this case: what happens in `SupportMailbox#process_reply` and `SupportMailbox#process_new_ticket` when an `inbound_email` is created via `ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!` *inside* a transactional test? Okay, even better, let's see how `SupportMailbox` behaves when `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` is raised within the `account.with_lock` block.

**HOLD IT! POSTGRESQL TRANSACTION ABORT ALERT!** This is big. Looking at `process_new_ticket` and `process_reply`: it seems that if a `Comment.create!` within an `account.with_lock` block inside a transactional test raises `RecordNotUnique`, *PostgreSQL will abort the entire outer transaction*. This is because `account.with_lock` uses `transaction` without setting `requires_new: true`. This causes `account.with_lock` to join the outer transaction. If a `RecordNotUnique` is raised inside this nested transaction, PostgreSQL will abort the *entire* transaction, which is not what we want!

Outside a transactional test, this isn't an issue. The `account.with_lock` starts its own transaction which rolls back cleanly if there's a `RecordNotUnique`. But in a transactional test, the nested transaction joins the outer transaction, and a `RecordNotUnique` becomes a catastrophic failure.

The solution? We need to ensure that `with_lock` or any locking mechanism uses `requires_new: true`. This sets a `SAVEPOINT` in the PostgreSQL transaction. Then, if `RecordNotUnique` happens, ONLY the savepoint rolls back, leaving the outer transaction healthy.

Now, let's consider `ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!` with `ActiveStorage::Blob` when `RecordNotUnique` happens in a transactional test. In that method, there's `create_and_upload_raw_email!` which runs *before* `create!`. The rescue clause catches `RecordNotUnique` and returns `nil`. But *wait*. Let's trace this! When a *duplicate* raw email is posted *twice* in the same integration test...

Here's the problem: when we use `Model.create!` inside `use_transactional_tests = true`, it doesn't create a savepoint in Rails 8. Rather, it calls `with_transaction_returning_status` and joins the outer transaction. If the `INSERT` hits a `PG::UniqueViolation`, PostgreSQL will abort the *entire* test transaction. What's worse is that `create_and_upload_raw_email!` will have run before this point, and now the database is in a failed transaction state!

**WHOA! THIS IS A HUGE DEAL.** This could be a major bug, so before we write ANY tests, we need to verify this hypothesis RIGHT NOW! We need a dedicated test file to replicate this issue and see how Rails 8.1.4 and PostgreSQL behave in this scenario.

arguments.command:
cd /app && bin/rails test -e '
require "test_helper"

class QuickRelayProbeTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  test "probe relay ingress sync processing and identical duplicate inside transactional test" do
    signup_and_verify!
    ActionMailer::Base.deliveries.clear

    raw = <<~EMAIL.gsub("\n", "\r\n")
      From: Alice <alice@example.test>
      To: acme@support.example.test
      Message-ID: <probe-1@example.test>
      Subject: Need help
      Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

      Hello support!
    EMAIL

    auth = ActionController::HttpAuthentication::Basic.encode_credentials("actionmailbox", "test-secret")
    headers = {
      "Authorization" => auth,
      "CONTENT_TYPE" => "message/rfc822"
    }

    with_env("RAILS_INBOUND_EMAIL_PASSWORD" => "test-secret") do
      post "/rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails", params: raw, headers: headers
      assert_response :no_content

      puts "Tickets after 1st post: #{Ticket.count}, InboundEmails: #{ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.pluck(:status)}"
      assert_equal 1, Ticket.count

      # Post identical raw email a second time!
      post "/rails/action_mailbox/relay/inbound_emails", params: raw, headers: headers
      assert_response :no_content

      puts "Tickets after 2nd identical post: #{Ticket.count}"
      assert_equal 1, Ticket.count
    end
  end
end
'

steps.reasoning_content:
**Deep Dive into Rails 8.1 Transactional Tests and SupportMailbox Robustness**

Okay, so Rails 8.1's `use_transactional_tests` is proving to be a game-changer with its automatic `SAVEPOINT` wrapping and `after_create_commit` firing. This is excellent for ensuring data consistency, especially with asynchronous processing. The initial synchronous `create!` and `after_create_commit` execution before the request completes is key. It's now crystal clear how the `RecordNotUnique` errors correctly roll back only the savepoint, leaving the test transaction pristine. And, the planned integration of `Account.transaction(requires_new: true)` within `SupportMailbox`'s `process_reply` and `process_new_ticket`, specifically around `account.lock!`, guarantees that any nested transactions that throw `RecordNotUnique` or `RecordInvalid` will ONLY roll back the savepoint, and not the entire transaction even in nested calls. That's a huge win for reliability.

But, before updating `SupportMailbox`, I need to scrutinize every potential edge case in `SupportMailbox#process_reply` and `process_new_ticket` as I'm integrating this new logic! What happens with a new email with invalid or same content/Message-ID that arrives with invalid content, and is then sent again after external fixes? Gotta make sure everything handles all scenarios gracefully.

Here's the detailed checklist I need to go through:

1.  **Subject Length:** Ensure subject truncation to 255 chars is safe.
2.  **Message-ID Normalization:** Verify that `Message-ID` normalization handles spaces, case, and edge cases correctly. Crucially, I have to ensure the existing `ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!` logic is working properly for duplicate messages, as well as if message-ID's are missing.
3.  **Missing `Message-ID`:** Test the behavior of a missing message ID and how the unique index works.
4.  **Complex `To:` and `Cc:` Addresses:** Test the various cases for address formats (quoted local-parts, multiple recipients with different domains, etc.)
5.  **`To:` and `Cc:` Address Combination:** Ensure that a "wrong token" in `Cc:` doesn't open a new ticket.
6.  **Valid `To:` and `Cc:` (reply-all):** Confirm correct routing when both a valid reply token and plain address are present.
7.  **Multiple Replies to Same Token:** Verify that only the requester can update the ticket, not a non-requester with the same token.
8.  **`From:` and `Reply-To:`:** Check that `From:` is used for sender identification (email address is lowercased).
9.  **Staff Reply via API:** Ensure that staff replies via `PATCH /api/v1/tickets/:id` from both admin and agent accounts correctly send emails for public replies, but not for private notes.
10. **Portal vs. Email Replies:** Confirm email sending behavior for staff replies after customer portal replies.
11. **`multipart/alternative` - Plain Text Priority:** Ensure `text/plain` is prioritized in `multipart/alternative` emails.
12. **HTML-Only Emails:** Handle HTML-only emails and ensure clean plain text extraction.
13. **Customized Email Settings:** Verify correct email addresses in `TicketMailer#staff_reply` with customized domain and from settings.

steps.message: I'll update `SupportMailbox` to use `Account.transaction(requires_new: true)` with `account.lock!` so any rescued unique/validation error safely rolls back only its savepoint.
steps.reasoning_content:
Okay, here's my take on those thoughts, tailored for an expert audience:

**Refining Transactional Integrity in Email Processing**

Alright, so the `mail.text_part` is handling inline content disposition beautifully; no surprises there, but always good to confirm that.

The key thought here is about reinforcing the transaction boundaries within the `SupportMailbox`. We need to ensure that the `account.lock!` operation within the `SupportMailbox`'s processing is absolutely bulletproof, especially given that email processing can often be nested within other transactions. A nested transaction could make recovery more complex. That's why I'm thinking of wrapping the `account.lock!` call within an `Account.transaction(requires_new: true)` block. This forces a new, independent transaction.

The benefit? We isolate the lock operation. If a `RecordNotUnique` or `RecordInvalid` exception occurs during the `lock!` call – which is a very real possibility in concurrent environments – the entire outer transaction won't be tainted. The rescue will gracefully rollback only the savepoint. That keeps our email processing reliable, predictable, and avoids cascading failures. Time to update `app/mailboxes/support_mailbox.rb` and get this protection in place.

arguments.command:
cd /app && ruby -e '
path = "/app/app/mailboxes/support_mailbox.rb"
content = File.read(path)
replaced = content.gsub("    account.with_lock do\n      account.reload", "    Account.transaction(requires_new: true) do\n      account.lock!")
raise "Expected 2 replacements" unless content.scan("    account.with_lock do\n      account.reload").size == 2
File.write(path, replaced)
' && git diff app/mailboxes/support_mailbox.rb || diff -u /dev/null /dev/null

**Expanding the Test Suite: A Deep Dive into Edge Cases**

Okay, so we've got a solid foundation with those initial tests – 74 tests, 2082 assertions, zero failures, errors or skips – but we can't stop there. We need to go much deeper and ensure this thing is robust. We are not going to leave any stone unturned.

First, the real-world scenarios: Let's hit it with a live Puma server test! Black-box HTTP tests, mimicking real interactions through `curl` and `Net::HTTP` in a test environment. Then, we need to test eager loading, running tests with `CI=true` and in a `production` environment to catch those autoloading and Zeitwerk issues before they hit production. We should also reload the database schema during testing to make sure our schema loads from scratch properly, and covers unique index cases.

Now, the fun part: the edge cases. We need to think like our users and anticipate every weird email they might throw at us.

*   **Handling Missing or Duplicate Message-IDs:** What if a user's email client doesn't include the `Message-ID`? How do we handle duplicate messages when the `Message-ID` is the same, even if the content might be slightly different? We need to make sure we don't create multiple tickets for the same message if the content is truly identical, even when the account is reactivated. Angle brackets on and off in the `Message-ID`?
